**Research note: PostgreSQL limits for schema and pool sizing**

**Identifier length.** By default, PostgreSQL identifiers (table names, column names and so on) can be at most 63 bytes. The lexical-structure docs say the system uses no more than NAMEDATALEN-1 bytes, and that NAMEDATALEN is 64 by default (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html). Longer names are not rejected. They are silently truncated to 63 bytes, so two long names that share a 63-byte prefix will collide. The limit is in bytes, not characters, so multi-byte UTF-8 names hit it sooner. You can raise it only by changing NAMEDATALEN in `src/include/pg_config_manual.h` and recompiling, which you won't want on managed Postgres. The "System limits" appendix confirms 63 bytes and says it can be increased by recompiling (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html).

**Columns per table.** The hard maximum is 1,600 columns. The appendix qualifies this: the practical limit can be lower, because a tuple must fit in a single 8192-byte heap page (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). Wide tables of fixed-width types (for example, many bigint or timestamp columns) will reach the page-size limit before 1,600 columns. Variable-length types such as text can be stored out of line (TOASTed), which eases the constraint, but I did not read a page that quantifies this. In practice, a table anywhere near this limit is a sign to split it or move some fields into a jsonb column.

**max_connections.** The default is typically 100. The connection-settings docs add that it might be lower if your kernel settings can't support it, as determined during initdb (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html). Managed services often override this default, so check the actual value on your target instance with `SHOW max_connections;`. Some of these connections are normally reserved for superuser access, which I did not verify on the pages I read. Leave headroom for migrations, monitoring and admin sessions.

**Recommendation.** Keep identifiers well under 63 bytes, ideally under about 50, and keep tables far narrower than 1,600 columns. Size the application pool, summed across all service instances, comfortably below max_connections (default 100). If you expect many instances or short-lived workers, put a pooler such as PgBouncer in front rather than raising max_connections.

{"answers": {"1": "63 bytes (NAMEDATALEN 64 minus 1)", "2": "1,600 (may be lower due to the 8192-byte page limit)", "3": "100 (typically)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html", "https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html"], "2": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html"]}}

**Research note: default memory and WAL settings in a fresh PostgreSQL install**

I read the current official PostgreSQL documentation for all three settings. The values below are quoted from those pages, not from memory.

**work_mem.** The default is 4MB (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). The limit applies per sort or hash operation, not per query or per connection. A complex query running many such operations in parallel across many sessions can therefore use many times this amount. That is why the default is conservative.

**shared_buffers.** The default is typically 128MB (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). The docs add that it might be lower if your kernel settings can't support 128MB, as determined during initdb. Check `SHOW shared_buffers;` on the actual install rather than assuming 128MB. It is a small value for any server with real RAM, and changing it requires a restart.

**max_wal_size.** The default is 1GB (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html). This is a soft limit on how large WAL can grow between automatic checkpoints. The same page gives the related min_wal_size default as 80MB (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html). If checkpoints are triggered by WAL volume rather than by time, the log will show it. That is the usual sign that max_wal_size is too low for the write load.

**Recommendation.** Raise shared_buffers well above 128MB, commonly around 25% of RAM on a dedicated server, and raise max_wal_size if the logs show frequent WAL-triggered checkpoints. Leave work_mem near its 4MB default globally and raise it per session or per role for heavy reporting queries, because the setting multiplies across concurrent operations.

{"answers": {"1": "4MB", "2": "128MB (typically; may be lower if kernel settings don't allow it)", "3": "1GB"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html"], "2": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html"]}}

DuckDB's default memory limit is 80% of RAM. SQLite's maximum database file is about 281 TB. MERGE first shipped in PostgreSQL 15.

**Research note: analytics side-store next to PostgreSQL**

**DuckDB memory.** DuckDB's configuration reference lists `memory_limit` with a default of 80% of RAM (source: https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/configuration/overview.html). If the side-store shares a host with PostgreSQL, that default can compete with PostgreSQL's shared buffers and OS cache. Set `memory_limit` explicitly in that case. I fetched the stable guide URL first, but it only redirected to the 2.0 docs, so I read the 2.0 page.

**SQLite file size.** The SQLite limits page says a database file can hold 4294967294 pages. At the maximum 65536-byte page size, that is about 2.8e+14 bytes, or 281 terabytes (source: https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html). At the default 4096-byte page size, the ceiling is about 17.5 TB, according to the same page. Either figure is far above what a typical analytics side-store needs, so file size shouldn't decide between the two.

**MERGE on PostgreSQL 15.** The PostgreSQL 15.0 release notes say "Add SQL MERGE command to adjust one table to match another". They describe it as similar to `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` but more batch-oriented (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/15.0/). The PostgreSQL 15 documentation also has a `MERGE` reference page (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/sql-merge.html). So MERGE is available on your PostgreSQL 15 and wasn't in any earlier major version. If any environment is still on PostgreSQL 14 or older, you'll need `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` or separate `UPDATE` and `INSERT` statements there.

**Recommendation.** Choose DuckDB for the analytics side-store, because it is built for columnar analytical queries. Cap its `memory_limit` if it runs on the same host as PostgreSQL. Use MERGE on PostgreSQL 15 for upserts and batch syncs, and keep SQLite for light, single-file local storage.

{"answers": {"1": "80% of RAM", "2": "about 281 TB (at 65536-byte pages; 4294967294 pages)", "3": "PostgreSQL 15"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/configuration/overview.html"], "2": ["https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/15.0/", "https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/sql-merge.html"]}}

**Research note: TLS version, DNS label length and HTTP 418**

**1. TLS 1.3.** TLS 1.3 was first specified in RFC 8446, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3". It was published in August 2018 as a Proposed Standard, and its abstract says it "specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446). That page now marks RFC 8446 as obsolete. The replacement is RFC 9846, which has the same title and is by the same author. It states "This document defines TLS version 1.3" and describes itself as a minor, backward-compatible update that keeps the version number. It obsoletes RFC 8446, RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) and several other TLS 1.2-era RFCs (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846). The page I read shows only a 2026 copyright, not a publication date. The answer to "which RFC specifies TLS 1.3" therefore depends on how current the guideline needs to be. RFC 8446 is the original and most widely cited one, and RFC 9846 is the current one.

**2. DNS label length.** A single DNS label is limited to 63 octets. RFC 1035, section 3.1, says the length field's six remaining bits "limit the label to 63 octets or less" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035). I did not read the full-name limit. It is a separate figure and should be checked against the same RFC before it goes into the guideline.

**3. HTTP "I'm a teapot".** The status code is 418, defined in RFC 2324, "Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0)". That RFC is an April Fools' document dated 1 April 1998, and RFC 7168 later updated it (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324). The code is a joke and is not part of the standard HTTP semantics. Services should not rely on it for real error handling.

**Recommendation.** Cite RFC 9846 as the current TLS 1.3 specification, and mention RFC 8446 as the original, so readers of older material can map between them. Require each host-name label to be at most 63 octets, and treat 418 as reserved or novelty, never as a status code the guideline asks services to return.

{"answers": {"1": "RFC 8446 (original); now obsoleted by RFC 9846", "2": "63 octets", "3": "418, RFC 2324"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446", "https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846"], "2": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035"], "3": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324"]}}

**Research note: platform limits for the deploy runbook**

**AWS Lambda timeout.** Lambda's documentation says the default timeout is 3 seconds. You can raise it in 1-second steps up to a maximum of 900 seconds (15 minutes) (source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html). The same page describes an exception: Lambda Managed Instances allow up to 5,400 seconds for asynchronous and event-source-mapping invocations (Amazon MQ and Amazon DocumentDB excluded). That exception does not apply to standard functions, so 900 seconds is the number for the runbook unless you use Managed Instances (source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html).

**Kubernetes termination grace period.** The Pod lifecycle documentation says: "The default `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting is 30 seconds." Pods get that long to shut down gracefully before they are killed (source: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/). It can be overridden per Pod in the spec. My first fetch of that page was truncated before the relevant section, so I read the remainder with an offset to get this quote.

**Docker default bridge subnet.** The default bridge `docker0` uses 172.17.0.0/16. The Mirantis documentation states: "The default IP range, or subnet, for `docker0` is `172.17.0.0/16`" (source: https://docs.mirantis.com/mke/current/install/plan-deployment/mcr-considerations/docker0.html). This is a vendor page, not Docker's own. I read several official Docker pages and none states the subnet as a default:
- The bridge driver page only shows example container addresses of 172.17.0.2 and 172.17.0.3 (https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/bridge/).
- The `dockerd` reference page gives no default value for `--bip` (https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/dockerd/).

The 172.17.0.x examples on the Docker bridge page are consistent with the Mirantis statement. Treat the figure as well established but not confirmed by a Docker page.

**Recommendation.** Set Lambda's timeout deliberately below 900 seconds, and make the service's shutdown work finish within Kubernetes' 30-second default. If it needs longer, raise `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` explicitly. For local Docker, say in the runbook that 172.17.0.0/16 is only the default and can clash with VPNs or corporate ranges. Tell people to set `bip` or `default-address-pools` in `daemon.json` if it does.

**Research note: test and tooling defaults**

**Vitest.** The default per-test timeout (`testTimeout`) is 5,000 ms when tests run in Node.js. If `browser.enabled` is true, the default rises to 15,000 ms (source: https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout). A repo that mixes Node and browser-mode projects will see two different defaults.

**Linux and Rust.** Linux 6.1 was the first mainline release with Rust support. The KernelNewbies page for that release says: "This release adds support for the Rust programming language," and describes it as initial support that later releases would improve (source: https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1). I also fetched the official kernel Rust documentation (https://docs.kernel.org/rust/index.html), but it doesn't name the first version, so I'm not citing it for this claim. I read only the first 100,000 of the roughly 239,000 characters on the KernelNewbies page. The Rust statement appeared in that part, but I didn't check the rest. The 6.1 support was only a starting point, so a team that actually writes kernel Rust will need a much newer kernel than 6.1.

**PostgreSQL.** The default `statement_timeout` is 0, which disables the timeout. The documentation says: "A value of zero (the default) disables the timeout." (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html). That page is the "current" docs, so it reflects the latest release, not necessarily the version you run.

**Recommendation.** Set vitest timeouts explicitly. Pick one value per project instead of relying on the 5 s Node default, and use a longer value for browser-mode projects. For PostgreSQL, set a non-zero `statement_timeout` for application roles, because the default lets a runaway query run forever. Treat 6.1 as the minimum kernel for Rust and pin the team's target to a recent release.

{"answers": {"1": "5000 ms (15000 ms if browser mode enabled)", "2": "Linux 6.1", "3": "0 (disabled)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout"], "2": ["https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html"]}}
